title: The Role of Test Engineering and Quality Fundamentals

questions.prompt: How does the modern definition describe Test Engineering?
options: A proactive QA discipline across the whole lifecycle, aimed at preventing defects
A reactive QC activity performed after implementation, focused on finding defects
A distinct downstream phase that starts only once all coding is complete
A process-auditing function that certifies teams against ISO standards
A developer-only practice limited to writing unit tests for each function
questions.explanation: The modern definition calls Test Engineering a proactive quality assurance discipline that spans the entire lifecycle and focuses on preventing defects; testing as a separate downstream phase describes the older waterfall role.

questions.prompt: Which description matches Quality Assurance (QA)?
options: Process-oriented activities such as policies, standards, audits and improvement loops
Product-oriented activities that evaluate whether a deliverable meets requirements
Dynamic evaluation of a product by executing it under specified conditions
Checking the conformance of the product to its specifications
Checking the product's fitness for purpose together with stakeholders
questions.explanation: QA is process-oriented and establishes confidence that quality will be achieved through policies, standards, audits and improvement loops; evaluating whether a specific deliverable meets requirements is Quality Control.

questions.prompt: According to the course's definition of testing, what does testing provide?
options: Information about risk and quality, not guarantees
A guarantee that no defects remain in the product
Formal proof that the product conforms to its specification
Confidence that the development process will achieve quality
A complete record of every possible input and its output
questions.explanation: Testing executes the product under specified conditions and observes outcomes, which provides information about risk and quality but no guarantees; building confidence in the process is what QA does.

questions.prompt: Before release, a team lets real end users try the product to check whether it actually fits their needs and purpose. Which activity is this?
options: Validation
Verification
Static testing
Unit testing
Quality assurance audit
questions.explanation: Validation asks 'Are we building the right product?' and checks fitness for purpose with stakeholders; verification only checks conformance to the specifications.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Quality Assurance (QA) and Quality Control (QC) is correct?
options: QA is proactive/preventive, while QC is reactive/detective
QA is reactive/detective, while QC is proactive/preventive
QA is product-oriented, while QC is process-oriented
QA is owned by QC personnel, while QC involves the entire organization
QA produces defect logs, while QC produces training materials
questions.explanation: The QA/QC comparison lists QA as proactive/preventive and process-oriented (the whole team's responsibility) and QC as reactive/detective and product-oriented (done by QC personnel).

questions.prompt: In the ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model, testability is listed as a sub-characteristic of which characteristic?
options: Maintainability
Reliability
Usability
Functional suitability
Portability
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 25010 lists testability under Maintainability, together with modularity, reusability, analyzability and modifiability.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a static testing activity?
options: Running a linter and SAST on the source code
Executing unit tests in the CI pipeline
Running a performance test on the system
Conducting user acceptance testing (UAT)
Running API/integration tests against a service
questions.explanation: Static testing evaluates artefacts without executing the code, and linters and SAST are listed static examples; unit, performance, UAT and API/integration tests execute the system, so they are dynamic.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of Equivalence Partitioning (EP)?
options: Group inputs into classes that behave alike and test one representative per class
Test the minimum, maximum and the values just inside and outside each limit
Enumerate combinations of conditions and the expected outcome of each one
Rank test items by likelihood, impact and detectability before testing them
Execute every possible input value to reach complete input coverage
questions.explanation: EP partitions inputs into classes expected to behave similarly and tests one representative from each class; testing the minimum, maximum and their neighbours is boundary value analysis.

questions.prompt: Which test design technique is meant for logic with multiple conditions, enumerating their combinations and expected outcomes?
options: Decision tables / cause-effect
Equivalence partitioning
Boundary value analysis
Risk-based testing
Exploratory testing
questions.explanation: Decision tables / cause-effect handle logic with multiple conditions by enumerating condition combinations and expected outcomes, minimized with pairwise where appropriate.

questions.prompt: A password must be 8–20 characters long. Which set of length equivalence classes matches the course's worked example?
options: <8 invalid, 8–20 valid, >20 invalid
<8 valid, 8–20 valid, >20 invalid
<8 invalid, 8–20 invalid, >20 valid
<7 invalid, 7–21 valid, >21 invalid
<8 invalid, 8–20 valid, >20 valid
questions.explanation: The worked example partitions length into <8 (invalid), 8–20 (valid) and >20 (invalid); 7 and 21 are boundary test values, not limits of the valid class.

questions.prompt: An input field accepts integers from 1 to 100. Testing just below, at and just above each boundary, which values does boundary value analysis select?
questions.explanation: BVA tests just below, at and just above each boundary: 0, 1, 2 around the minimum and 99, 100, 101 around the maximum; leaving out 2 and 99 misses the just-inside values.

questions.prompt: Using the course's risk-based testing rubric, a feature is rated likelihood 4, impact 5 and detectability 2. What is its RPN?
questions.explanation: RPN = Likelihood × Impact × Detectability = 4 × 5 × 2 = 40; 20 ignores detectability and 11 adds the scores instead of multiplying them.

questions.prompt: On the 1–5 risk-based testing rubric, what does a detectability score of 5 mean?
options: Hard to detect until production
Easy to detect before release
Frequent in the field or code-change area
Safety, financial or regulatory breach
Cosmetic impact only
questions.explanation: On the rubric, detectability 1 means easy to detect pre-release and 5 means hard to detect until production, so a higher detectability score raises the risk.

questions.prompt: In the risk assessment matrix, what risk level results from a Remote (D) probability combined with Catastrophic (1) severity?
options: Serious
High
Medium
Low
Eliminated
questions.explanation: In the matrix, Remote (D) with Catastrophic (1) is rated Serious; Catastrophic severity becomes High only at Occasional (C) or a more frequent probability.

questions.prompt: How does the test engineer's role differ between sequential (waterfall) and incremental development?
options: Waterfall: testing is a distinct downstream phase; incremental: testers take part repeatedly across increments
Waterfall: testers take part repeatedly across increments; incremental: testing is a distinct downstream phase
Waterfall: regression testing is central; incremental: regression testing is no longer needed
Waterfall: early feedback becomes possible; incremental: feedback waits until deployment
Waterfall: testers sit in cross-functional teams; incremental: testing starts after deployment
questions.explanation: In waterfall, testing is a distinct downstream phase; in incremental development, software is developed and tested in increments, so testers participate repeatedly, regression testing becomes important and early feedback is possible.

questions.prompt: How does the test engineer's position change in Agile and DevOps environments?
options: Test engineers become integrated members of cross-functional teams
Test engineers form a separate team that tests after implementation
Test engineers test only once the full release has been completed
Test engineers focus on manual testing and avoid test automation
Test engineers join the project only during the maintenance phase
questions.explanation: With CI/CD, continuous testing, test automation and shift-left testing, test engineers in Agile and DevOps become integrated members of cross-functional teams rather than a separate downstream group.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility is listed under a modern test engineer's Quality Assurance focus?
options: Establishing quality gates and exit criteria
Reviewing overnight CI/CD test results
Developing test automation frameworks
Conducting exploratory testing sessions
Managing test data and test environments
questions.explanation: Establishing quality gates and exit criteria is listed under the Quality Assurance focus; reviewing overnight CI/CD results is a daily activity, while automation frameworks, exploratory testing and test data/environments are technical activities.

questions.prompt: In the testing pyramid, which description fits the base layer?
options: Unit tests: many tests, fast execution, low cost
Integration tests: moderate number, medium speed and cost
System/E2E tests: fewer tests, slower execution, higher cost
Unit tests: fewer tests, slower execution, higher cost
System/E2E tests: many tests, fast execution, low cost
questions.explanation: The base of the pyramid is unit tests: many tests, fast execution and low cost; fewer, slower and costlier tests belong to the System/E2E top, and integration tests sit in the middle.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes unit testing?
options: Done by developers, mostly white-box, with mocked dependencies
Done by an independent test team in a production-like environment
Done by business users to validate the business requirements
Done by external users in their own real environment
Done on the complete integrated application across browsers
questions.explanation: Unit testing is performed by developers, primarily white-box, in a development environment with mocked dependencies; an independent team in a production-like environment describes system testing.

questions.prompt: A team integrates the low-level modules first and writes drivers to call them. Which integration strategy is this?
options: Bottom-up
Top-down
Big Bang
Sandwich/Hybrid
System integration
questions.explanation: Bottom-up integration starts with low-level modules and uses drivers; top-down starts with top-level modules and uses stubs, and Big Bang integrates all modules simultaneously.

questions.prompt: During system testing, a tester runs the application on several browsers and operating systems. Which type of system testing is this?
options: Compatibility testing
Usability testing
Performance testing
Security testing
Functional testing
questions.explanation: Compatibility testing covers different browsers and operating systems; performance covers response times, throughput and scalability, and usability covers user experience and interface design.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes beta testing from alpha testing?
options: Beta uses external users in a real environment; alpha is internal testing by the organization
Beta is internal testing by the organization; alpha uses external users in a real environment
Beta is the final validation by business users; alpha is unit testing by developers
Beta tests interactions between modules; alpha tests the complete integrated system
Beta is done by an independent test team; alpha is done by external end users
questions.explanation: Alpha testing is internal testing by the organization, while beta testing uses external users in a real environment; final validation by business users is User Acceptance Testing (UAT).

questions.prompt: According to the course's ethics guidance, how should test engineers handle Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in test data?
options: Use masked or synthetic data where possible
Copy unmodified production data for realism
Include real PII in reports for traceability
Keep PII unmasked but only in test environments
Avoid documenting assumptions about the data
questions.explanation: The ethics guidance says to respect privacy and PII by using masked or synthetic data where possible, and to document residual risk and assumptions explicitly.
